content: Adolescent substance use is a significant issue, not only as a standalone problem but also because it serves as a risk factor for other problematic behaviors. Substance use during adolescence can result in serious and often long-term health and social consequences. Therefore, early intervention is critical to prevent the escalation of substance use into more severe problems. Brief interventions (BIs) have demonstrated efficacy in reducing problematic substance use among adolescents, particularly for those with moderately risky patterns of use. These interventions can be effectively implemented in school settings. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of brief school-based interventions in reducing substance use and other related behavioral outcomes among adolescents, as compared to other interventions or assessment-only conditions. The original literature search was conducted in March 2013, with an update performed in February 2015. The search included 10 electronic databases, six websites focused on evidence-based interventions, and reference lists of relevant studies and reviews from 1966 to February 2015. Additionally, authors and organizations were contacted to identify any further studies. The review included randomized controlled trials that evaluated the effects of brief school-based interventions for adolescents who use substances. The primary outcomes assessed were the reduction or cessation of substance use, while secondary outcomes included engagement in criminal activity and other delinquent or problem behaviors associated with substance use. Standard methodological procedures, including the GRADE approach, were used to evaluate the quality of evidence. Six trials involving 1,176 adolescents were included in the review, with outcomes measured at various follow-up periods. Three studies (732 adolescents) compared brief interventions to information provision only, while three studies (444 adolescents) compared brief interventions to assessment-only conditions. The quality of evidence was downgraded due to risks of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency in the included studies. The studies primarily focused on alcohol and cannabis use. When compared to information provision only, moderate-quality evidence indicated that brief interventions did not significantly affect substance use outcomes at short-, medium-, or long-term follow-up. Similarly, no significant effects were observed on delinquent behaviors among adolescents. However, when compared to assessment-only conditions, lowor very low-quality evidence suggested that brief interventions reduced cannabis use frequency at short-term follow-up in one study (SMD -0.83; 95% CI -1.14 to -0.53, n = 269). At medium-term follow-up, brief interventions significantly reduced the frequency of alcohol use (SMD -0.91; 95% CI -1.21 to -0.61, n = 242), alcohol abuse (SMD -0.38; 95% CI -0.70 to -0.07, n = 190), alcohol dependence (SMD -0.58; 95% CI -0.90 to -0.26, n = 190), and cannabis abuse (SMD -0.34; 95% CI -0.65 to -0.02, n = 190) in one study. At long-term follow-up, brief interventions reduced alcohol abuse (SMD -0.72; 95% CI -1.05 to -0.40, n = 181), cannabis use frequency (SMD -0.56; 95% CI -0.75 to -0.36, n = 181), cannabis abuse (SMD -0.62; 95% CI -0.95 to -0.29, n = 181), and cannabis dependence (SMD -0.96; 95% CI -1.30 to -0.63, n = 181) in one study. However, the overall quality of evidence for these comparisons was low. The effects of brief interventions on delinquent or problem behaviors were mixed, but one study found a significant effect at long-term follow-up (SMD -0.78; 95% CI -1.11 to -0.45). In conclusion, there is lowor very low-quality evidence suggesting that brief school-based interventions may be more effective than assessment-only conditions in reducing alcohol and cannabis use, with these reductions sustained at long-term follow-up. However, moderate-quality evidence indicates that brief interventions likely do not have a significant effect on substance use outcomes when compared to information provision. It is too early to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of brief school-based interventions for reducing adolescent substance use. Further high-quality research is needed to evaluate the relative effectiveness of these interventions, particularly in lowand middle-income countries.
